rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation is a very safe destination for transgender visitors in practice, with a legal framework that lags behind. There is no national anti-discrimination law — a 2023 law in this area is symbolic — and legal gender change still requires a court process. But courts have moved in trans people's favour: the top court struck down the sterilisation requirement for legal gender change in 2023 and ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal the same year. If a trans visitor is arrested or detained here, the custody consequence of the lagging framework is documented rather than theoretical: facilities house inmates by their family-register (registered) sex rather than gender identity — a women's prison held an inmate registered female who identifies as a man, and a transgender activist was held among men for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention, initially denied hormone treatment, mocked for his identity during interrogations, and allowed to shower away from other detained men only after requests, with hormones arriving only after a doctor recommended them. State/province-level pressure over an inmate's male clothing and hairstyle went unresolved for years before a bar association issued a formal warning to the prison in September 2023.

Day-to-day risk is minimal: violent crime is rare, visibly trans visitors report curiosity more often than hostility, hotels and transport are unproblematic, and the capital and the second city have an established queer scene. The main practical challenge is the strictly gendered, full-nudity culture of hot springs — manageable using guides to gender-neutral or private rental baths and mixed open-air baths, which travellers actively share.

Same-sex marriage remains unavailable, which matters for a trans visitor planning to travel with a partner on spousal status. One caveat: online transphobic rhetoric and misinformation rose visibly during the 2023 legislative debates, indicating a live culture-war current, though it rarely translates into street-level trouble for visitors.

A dated 2009 shadow report documents invisibility, marginalisation, silent prejudice and stigmatisation plus discrimination across education, employment, housing and health care with little governmental attention at the time — a baseline for comparing how far institutional protection has moved.

Custody-policy flux surrounds the placement practice: a bar association's September 2023 formal 'warning' to the prison followed years with no policy change on an inmate's male clothing and hairstyle, and an international human-rights organisation (June 2025) frames the pre-trial detention of a transgender activist — held among men, initially denied hormone treatment until a doctor recommended it — within its broader criticism of the nation's general pre-trial detention system, a burden every detainee faces that falls harder on a transgender detainee.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation is one of the most accepting destinations for transgender visitors. Visible gender variance is part of mainstream culture (a long-standing local tradition long predates modern categories), the government actively promotes LGBTQ tourism, same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025 as the first in the region, and the border authority runs a dedicated initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender. Gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The gaps are legal rather than social: there is still no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, the 2015 gender-equality act is weakly enforced, and — as the 2025 murder of a trans woman in a resort city highlighted — the nation has no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime. The gap extends into custody: because no document of this nation can identify a trans woman as female, placement follows legal sex in documented cases — a trans activist who became a detainee while protesting the junta in June 2015 was sent to a men's prison, told "she remains a man" and harassed during intake — while the prison authority says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993, holds transgender inmates in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men at one remand prison, and accepts that transgender women elsewhere usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary confinement. A trans visitor detained here therefore meets an unresolved placement practice: birth-sex men's facilities in documented cases, separated LGBT wings in others, with no guaranteed identity-matched housing.

For a visitor the practical risks are mostly the nation's general ones: nightlife disputes, scams, and alcohol-fuelled incidents, with some reported friction in resort nightlife districts. Everyday movement, hotels, healthcare, and transit are unproblematic.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Same-sex marriage legal since January 2025 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

Custody-policy flux: after reports of abuse and the documented placement of a trans woman in a men's prison in 2015, the prison authority announced a pilot using a prison in the capital as an LGBT facility — reported in 2016-17 as a possible world-first exclusively-LGBTQ prison — which activists welcomed while fearing it "could encourage exclusion" and insisting placement "should be an option, not an obligation"; authority counts at the time recorded roughly 4,448 LGBT-identified prisoners among about 300,000 prisoners (34 of them transgender), with a 2017 figure of more than 6,000 registered as sexual minorities.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation is the most progressive destination for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and a major city serving as a regional queer hub. The protections do not reliably reach custody: documentation shows the nation's response to transgender-prisoner vulnerability has been isolation or segregation from the general prison population rather than placement in facilities matching gender identity, and trans women have at times been held in men's prisons — but courts have intervened case-by-case, most notably an October 2019 ruling that ordered the prison service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one.

Two traveler-specific risks pull the score down. First, the main international airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition ("If you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male"). Every foreign visitor transits it, making this a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people "bearing the brunt." Anti-trans rhetoric from a foreign political leader is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

The right-wing governing coalition and the war aftermath have weakened protections, though a parliamentary security committee has convened on LGBTQ public-space security.
rewrites.blindTangential:

rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation is one of the most socially accepting destinations in the region for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity, a vibrant Pride scene in the capital, and no criminalisation — trans identity has never been criminalised in this country.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (so identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender), an anti-discrimination equality bill — a national anti-discrimination law — has been stalled for 25 years, and there is no marriage equality. Documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The national human-rights commission actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction and genuinely warm social acceptance, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue — documented incidents include bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials; partner or marriage-based protections do not exist. The vacuum extends into custody: transgender women at the capital's main city jail are held by birth sex in the ordinary male dormitories — where mandatory head-shaving applies on arrival to the male dorm and safety comes from inmate hierarchies rather than any gender-matched placement policy — while another city's jail answers abuse risk by relocating LGBT detainees to a separate annex; a trans visitor arrested here has no documented path to identity-matched custody.
rewrites.blindTangential:

This is national legislation flux that may colour a visit, not a direct travel restriction.

Custody-policy flux: the documented official response is administrative segregation rather than gender-matched placement — a jail authority's community-relations chief said LGBT detainees at one city's jail are relocated in batches to the jail annex "to prevent abuse", alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings living in the annex since its establishment (March 2023); an investigative-journalism investigation (December 2022) documents that at the capital's main city jail transgender women and gay men held in the ordinary male dormitories use informal same-sex "weddings" with male inmates as a survival and protection strategy against abuse.

The custody axis completes the picture: the nation operates no prison system — only a few cells used for pre-trial detention — and persons sentenced to imprisonment by the nation serve their time in another nation's prisons with costs covered by the nation, so there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case in this jurisdiction; any custodial consequence for a visitor would be served in another nation's prison system, outside this record's scope.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — the country has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 periodic human-rights review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted an independent international expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2023. The nation's two main cities have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: a human-rights organisation documents "shocking" harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially. The consequence axis of an arrest is thinly documented and cannot be read as a protected standard: the only placement finding is a February 2025 statement by the president of the national human-rights committee, made in praise of a women's correctional centre, that transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from the men's facility to the women's facility — a surgery-gated practice with no statute or formal policy text cited. Nothing is documented on placement for trans prisoners who have not had surgery, and no trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is on record; with no legal gender recognition, a detained trans visitor's placement would default to birth sex absent the surgery-gated transfer — a gap that cannot be assumed safe even though the country's non-criminalising framework keeps arrest itself unlikely.

The cooperative posture carries an unfulfilled-promise edge: the country also accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage (2019 review) and seven on marriage equality (2024 review), and legislation still contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions — a reform-promise layer rather than a visitor-facing restriction.

The same report flags that prison overcrowding has worsened because of gang-crackdown arrests — the custody context in which any placement decision would operate, resident-facing rather than a visitor-facing restriction.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation is dangerous for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 penal code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and an international rights body lists the nation as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and "cheating by personation" provisions against trans people. An international jurists' commission identifies the national police as "the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals" — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. The capital has a small organised community and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.

The consequence axis makes the danger concrete: as of October 2024 the prison department has no dedicated transgender housing — its media spokesperson/Commissioner said current facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, with separate accommodation only planned for prisons built in the future — and placement defaults to birth sex in the current male/female ward system, with a discretionary, medicalised exception route: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender 'where possible', while those without it undergo a doctor's assessment of whether they 'can be considered a transgender' before placement, with the inmate's preference weighed. Officials also cite the fear of people accused of sex offences 'identifying as transgender' to enter female housing with born-male offenders as a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. A detained trans visitor — unlikely to hold the recognition card, in a country where police already use vagrancy and personation provisions against trans people — would default to birth-sex placement under a practice with no statutory rule and no dedicated housing.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Sections 365/365A criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the vagrancy and "personation" provisions are the trans-specific enforcement vehicle.

Placement-framework context: a prisoners'-rights committee is calling for future prisons to give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that 'developed countries have recognised transgender rights' — advocacy positioning around the documented birth-sex default rather than a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:

rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the historic buggery laws (2018 legal challenge, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still "beaten, stoned and chopped," with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of dating-app ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including one man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.

The consequence axis of an arrest is acknowledged in official terms as unsafe: the 2018 gender-equality protocol for judicial officers says plainly that "there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities". The only mechanism is a judicial officer's sentencing recommendation that prison authorities make provisions for the inmate's physical safety, and the Protocol's other directives — courts to refer to intersex/transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and permit court access irrespective of dress — govern court process rather than custody placement. Placement for a detained trans visitor is therefore discretionary, with no dedicated facility, special unit or statutory placement standard on record; the documented official position is that the penal system cannot safely accommodate trans prisoners.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation is dangerous for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed a bill on human sexual rights and family values: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for "promotion." The president refused to assent pending legal challenges, the top court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected. That reintroduction materialised in late May 2026, when parliament passed a new bill on human sexual rights and family values: up to three years' imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, longer terms for promotion/advocacy, and a 'duty to report' prohibited acts to police — passed under pressure from religious leaders on the current president, whose ratification is still required and widely expected.

Under existing law, "unnatural carnal knowledge" carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The capital has a resilient underground community — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks — but nothing that can protect a visitor.

The consequence axis of an arrest is the direct official pathway this bill creates: if ratified, identity alone becomes an imprisonable offence for the population that any prison-placement practice would apply to. Neither the 2026 reporting nor any source in this record contains a provision on how such prisoners would be housed, and no national prison placement rule, trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is publicly documented. In a nation that criminalises identity and lacks legal gender recognition, with documented mob violence, an undocumented placement practice cannot be assumed safe: a detained trans visitor would be held under a system with no documented housing standard and no documented recourse.
